questions.question: Name the seven body systems studied in Grade 9 and give the main function of each in one clause.
questions.expected_answer: Digestive: breaks food into soluble molecules such as glucose and absorbs them. Circulatory: transports oxygen, nutrients, wastes and heat in the blood. Respiratory: takes oxygen into the blood and removes carbon dioxide. Excretory: filters the blood and removes urea, excess water and salts as urine. Nervous: receives information and coordinates and controls responses and the other systems. Musculoskeletal: supports, protects and moves the body. Reproductive: produces sex cells and, in females, carries the developing baby.

questions.question: Trace the path of oxygen and glucose from the air and a slice of bread to a thigh muscle cell, and the path of the carbon dioxide and urea produced, naming the system responsible at each step.
questions.expected_answer: Digestive system digests starch to glucose and absorbs it into the blood in the small intestine; respiratory system takes oxygen into the blood in the alveoli; circulatory system (heart and blood vessels) carries both to the capillaries of the thigh, where they diffuse into the cell and respiration occurs in the mitochondria. Carbon dioxide diffuses into the blood, is carried by the circulatory system to the lungs and breathed out by the respiratory system; urea (made in the liver) is carried by the blood to the kidneys and removed by the excretory system in urine.

questions.question: Explain, as a chain, how asthma in the respiratory system causes a person's muscles to tire quickly, and why the circulatory system must appear in the answer.
questions.expected_answer: Asthma narrows the airways so less oxygen enters the blood in the lungs; the circulatory system therefore carries less oxygen to the muscle cells; with less oxygen the mitochondria release less energy from glucose; so the muscles tire quickly although they are healthy. The circulatory system must appear because oxygen reaches muscles only by transport in the blood; the lungs never supply muscles directly.
